quickAnswer: Nationally, multi-story exterior office window cleaning costs about $0.20 to $0.75 per square foot of glass, $8 to $25 per pane, or $55 to $95 per technician hour, depending on whether the crew uses water-fed poles, lifts, rope access, or a building maintenance unit. Expect a mobilization minimum of $750 to $2,500 per visit for anything above three stories.

blocks.text: How Multi-Story Window Cleaning Is Priced

Unlike nightly janitorial service, which is priced per square foot of floor area, exterior window cleaning on a multi-story office is priced against the glass itself and the method needed to reach it. Contractors use three unit structures: price per square foot of glass surface, price per pane or per fixture, and price per technician hour. Most commercial bids start from a per-pane or per-square-foot estimate built from elevation drawings, then add a mobilization charge for rigging, lift rental, or equipment setup. Understanding which unit a vendor uses is the first step to comparing bids that otherwise look impossible to reconcile.

blocks.text: Ranges assume standard commercial glass with routine soil. Per-pane pricing assumes panes of roughly 20 to 40 sq ft; oversized curtain-wall lites are almost always quoted per square foot instead. Hourly rates sit within the specialty band of $55 to $95 per hour, compared with $35 to $65 per hour for standard janitorial labor, because high-access technicians carry fall-protection certifications and higher insurance costs.
Worked Example: Budgeting a Five-Story Office

Consider a five-story, 60,000 sq ft office with about 18,000 sq ft of exterior glass across four elevations. A rope-access crew quotes $0.42 per sq ft, which equals $7,560 per full exterior cleaning. The vendor adds no separate mobilization because the job exceeds its $1,500 minimum. If the building cleans exterior glass twice a year, the annual spend is $15,120. Spread across the floor area, that is about $0.25 per sq ft of floor space per year, or roughly $0.021 per sq ft per month, a useful figure to compare against your nightly janitorial rate of $0.05 to $0.10 per sq ft per visit for a building of that size.

items: Glass area: measure from elevation drawings or ask the vendor to provide a takeoff; a curtain wall is often 40 to 60 percent of the gross facade.
Both sides or exterior only: interior-side cleaning of perimeter glass adds 30 to 50 percent and requires furniture clearance on every floor.
Frames, mullions, and sills: detailing adds roughly $0.05 to $0.10 per sq ft of glass.
Skylights, canopies, and atrium glass: usually separately quoted because access differs from the main elevations.
Hard-water or construction residue: restoration is project work priced per pane after a test area.

blocks.title: Quick sanity check for any bid
blocks.text: Divide the total per-visit price by the square feet of glass. If the result falls below $0.20 on a building above three stories, ask what is excluded. If it exceeds $0.75 without a BMU, unusual glass, or heavy restoration, ask for the labor-hour breakdown.

Mobilization covers rigging inspection, roof anchor certification checks, lift delivery, sidewalk barricades, and crew travel. For small multi-story buildings, the minimum often exceeds the unit-rate math. A three-story office with 3,000 sq ft of glass at $0.28 per sq ft computes to $840, but if the vendor needs a lift, the $1,200 minimum governs. Bundling exterior glass with the annual cleaning of another building in your portfolio, or scheduling on the same day as a neighboring property, is the most reliable way to spread mobilization costs.

blocks.title: Fall protection and anchor certification
blocks.text: Federal OSHA walking-working surface rules require building owners to certify in writing that rope-descent anchorages are inspected and capable of supporting the required loads before rope access work begins, with periodic re-inspection. Ask whether the vendor's quote includes anchor inspection or assumes your building already has current certification, and require a certificate of insurance naming owner and manager as additional insured.

items.name: Height and access method
items.text: Each step from pole to lift to rope access to BMU raises per-square-foot rates because crews are smaller, slower, and more highly certified.

items.name: Facade complexity
items.text: Setbacks, overhangs, sunshades, and curved glass slow descent lines and add repositioning time.

items.name: Ground conditions
items.text: Sidewalks needing barricades, landscaping below drop zones, and parking that must be closed all add labor and permit costs.

items.name: Frequency
items.text: Glass cleaned quarterly carries less soil and typically earns a lower unit rate than glass cleaned once a year.

items.name: Season and weather windows
items.text: Rope and swing-stage work stops in high winds and freezing temperatures, so spring and fall slots fill fast and command firmer pricing.

blocks.text: Coordinating Exterior Glass With Interior Floor Programs

Exterior window projects often happen on the same weekend as interior periodic work, since the building is already staffed for access. That makes it a good time to schedule perimeter carpet extraction, which picks up grit that falls inside when windows are opened or interior glass is cleaned. A Mytee Lite 8070, a 4-gallon heated extractor with a 120 PSI pump and 1000-watt heater, suits perimeter offices on a mid-size floor. For hard-floor lobbies and elevator landings, a Bissell Commercial BGEM9000 random-orbit machine with a 13-inch pad is low-vibration enough for occupied-hour touchups, while a Powr-Flite M171-3 17-inch 175 RPM rotary handles scrubbing and stripping VCT in service corridors. Ask your janitorial vendor to price these as a combined periodic visit.
Converting Quotes Into an Annual Budget

Most multi-story offices clean exterior glass two to four times a year. Multiply the per-visit price by visits, add any separate interior-side or frame detailing, and include a 5 to 10 percent contingency for weather rescheduling or added restoration. Present ownership with the annual number and the per-sq-ft equivalent so it can be compared with janitorial and other building service lines.

faqs.q: What is the average cost to clean exterior windows on a multi-story office?
faqs.a: Most US bids fall between $0.20 and $0.75 per square foot of glass or $8 to $25 per pane, with minimums of $750 to $2,500 above three stories. A five-story office with 18,000 sq ft of glass typically pays $5,000 to $10,000 per full exterior cleaning.

faqs.q: Is per-pane or per-square-foot pricing better for buyers?
faqs.a: Per-square-foot pricing is more transparent for curtain walls and oversized lites. Per-pane pricing works well for punched windows of consistent size. Either way, require the vendor to state the quantity used so bids can be normalized.

faqs.q: Does the building owner have safety obligations for rope access work?
faqs.a: Yes. Under OSHA walking-working surface rules, owners must provide written certification that rope-descent anchorages have been inspected and can support required loads. Vendors should also provide a certificate of insurance and fall-protection training records.

faqs.q: How does exterior window cost compare with monthly janitorial cost?
faqs.a: Annualized exterior window cleaning often equals about $0.01 to $0.03 per sq ft of floor area per month. Janitorial service at 4.333 weeks per month runs far higher, so window cleaning is a relatively small but visible line item.

faqs.q: Are cleaning chemicals for high-rise windows regulated?
faqs.a: Vendors must keep Safety Data Sheets for detergents and any restoration compounds under OSHA Hazard Communication. Buildings pursuing green certifications may require Green Seal or Safer Choice glass cleaners and controls on runoff to storm drains.
